Bauhaus: A modernist design movement that emphasizes basic geometric shapes, functional layouts, and stark typography over ornament.
Risograph: A stencil-based printing process known for distinct paper textures, limited spot colors, and slightly misaligned layers.
non-autoregressive: A model architecture that outputs predictions all at once in a single pass instead of generating text token by token.
calibration: The degree to which an AI model's stated confidence score reflects the actual mathematical probability of being correct.
tracking pixel: A tiny snippet of code added to a website to log visitors' activity and report it back to an advertising platform.
SameSite cookie: A browser security setting that determines whether a stored cookie is sent along with requests coming from third-party sites.
open-weight: An AI model whose trained internal numbers are released for anyone to download and run locally, rather than being locked behind an API.
VAE: Variational Autoencoder, a component in image generation models that translates compressed mathematical representations back into visible pixels.
model weights: The mathematical parameters inside a trained neural network that define its behavior and knowledge.
distillation: Training a new AI model by feeding it the outputs and reasoning produced by an existing model.
Overton window: The range of ideas and policies considered acceptable to the mainstream public at a given time.
ALPR: Automated License Plate Recognition, a system that uses cameras and image processing to track vehicle plates.
progenitor cell: An early stem-like cell that is committed to dividing and differentiating into a specific type of mature tissue.
in vitro: Studies or biological processes carried out in laboratory glassware or culture dishes rather than inside a living organism.
hindbrain: The lower back region of the brain that coordinates motor controls and vital involuntary functions like breathing.
sandbox: An isolated digital container where untested or untrusted code can run safely without affecting the rest of the computer or network.
orchestrator: A tool that automates the scheduling, scaling, and networking of many computing jobs across a cluster of servers.
UUID: A universally unique identifier, used in Bluetooth communications to advertise specific services or hardware models to nearby devices.
web-seed: A regular web server link included inside a torrent, allowing users to download files even if no other peers are currently sharing them.
SHA-256: A cryptographic hashing algorithm that produces a unique fingerprint for a file, used to verify the data was not modified or corrupted.
abliterated: A method of modifying an AI model's internal weights to bypass safety filters and refusal behavior.
HBM: High Bandwidth Memory, a 3D-stacked DRAM design that provides extremely fast data transfer speeds for AI hardware.
Glass carrier: A rigid temporary glass backing that holds a silicon wafer flat so it will not warp or snap while being ground down.
DRAM: Dynamic Random-Access Memory, the standard working memory used in computers, phones, and graphics cards.
mirror domain: An alternative web address that serves identical copies of a website, often used to bypass blocks or share network traffic.
Tetris effect: A psychological phenomenon where dedicating hours to an activity causes you to involuntarily see its patterns in everyday life and dreams.
doomscrolling: Compulsively scrolling through endless feeds of depressing or alarming news on a screen.
private equity: Investment funds that pool capital to buy privately held businesses or take public companies private, aiming to streamline operations and sell them later for a profit.
management services organization: A third-party business entity that handles administrative, non-clinical operations and billing for healthcare providers.
treble damages: A statutory remedy where a court awards a winning plaintiff up to three times the amount of actual financial damages suffered.
linear content: Traditional television programming that runs on a set broadcast schedule rather than on demand.
EULA: End-user license agreement, the legal contract between a software or service provider and the customer using it.
SPARC: A processor architecture created by Sun Microsystems for its workstations and enterprise servers.
Solaris: A Unix operating system developed by Sun Microsystems to run on SPARC and x86 computers.
x86: The standard family of computer processor designs that dominates modern personal computers and servers.
reinforcement learning: A machine learning training method where a model learns by taking actions and receiving rewards or penalties.
prompt caching: Reusing previously processed prompt data so an AI provider does not have to recompute identical text on every request.
jailbreak: A prompt designed to trick an AI model into bypassing its built-in safety rules and content filters.
motivated explanation: An explanation designed to show why a mathematical idea or definition was chosen in the first place, rather than just mechanically verifying that it works.
Lean: A programming language and proof assistant used by mathematicians to formally verify that mathematical proofs contain no logical errors.
futures: Financial contracts where a buyer agrees to purchase a specific amount of a good at a set price on a future date.
ADFGVX cipher: A World War I field cipher used by the German army that combines letter substitution on a grid with a column transposition step.
LoRA: A parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique that freezes the original model weights and trains a much smaller set of adapter weights.
Brier score: A metric that scores the accuracy of probabilistic forecasts, where lower values indicate more accurate and confident probabilities.
Gated DeltaNet: A linear recurrent attention layer used in hybrid models to process sequences efficiently without full quadratic attention.
cmudict: An open-source pronunciation dictionary for English that maps words to sequences of phonetic sounds.
trie: A tree-shaped data structure commonly used to store and quickly look up strings based on their prefixes.
LLM: A large language model, which is an AI system trained on vast amounts of text to predict and generate language.
pairing mode: A temporary state where a wireless device broadcasts a beacon so nearby phones or computers can discover and connect to it.
adventure games: A video game genre focused on exploration, storytelling, and solving inventory or dialogue puzzles rather than fast reflexes.
Lua: A lightweight, embeddable scripting language widely used by game developers to write game logic.
RTS: Real-time strategy, a video game genre where players build bases and command armies simultaneously rather than taking turns.
Elo: A mathematical rating system used to rank competitors or AI models based on head-to-head game results.
priors: Your existing assumptions or beliefs before taking new evidence into account.
failure mode: The specific way or predictable pattern in which a system or plan breaks down.
MCP: Model Context Protocol, an open standard created to let AI assistants connect to external tools, databases, and services.
context bloat: When an AI model's working memory fills up with schemas and system instructions, leaving less room to process the actual task.
thinking tokens: Hidden tokens generated during an AI's internal reasoning phase before it returns an answer.
inference regime: The specific serving configuration, hardware limits, and compute budget allocated to run an AI query.
CRT: Cathode Ray Tube, an older display technology that shot electron beams at phosphors on a glass screen, producing distinctive scanlines and slight color bleed.
Dithering: An artistic technique of placing alternating pixel patterns side by side to trick the eye into seeing new colors or smooth gradients on limited hardware.
Anti-aliasing: Smoothing jagged, stair-stepped pixel edges by placing pixels with intermediate color shades along high-contrast borders.
open weights: An AI model whose underlying trained parameters are made available for anyone to download and run directly.
activated parameters: The specific slice of a model's total neural network weights calculated during a given request.
Lean formalization: Translating mathematical proofs into code so a computer proof assistant can verify that every logical step is strictly correct.
Computer Algebra System: Software designed to manipulate mathematical equations symbolically rather than just calculating numeric answers.
micropayments: Very small financial transactions, often just a few cents or fractions of a cent.
gamification: Using game mechanics like points, badges, and streaks in ordinary tasks to motivate behavior.
allocator: A component in code responsible for requesting, assigning, and freeing blocks of computer memory.
destructor: A routine that runs automatically to clean up a variable's memory when it goes out of scope.
carbon capture: Technologies that trap carbon dioxide emissions at the source before they can enter the atmosphere.
particulate matter: Microscopic specks of solid or liquid material suspended in the air that can cause respiratory issues.
